abstract.p: RNK08954, an oral and selective KRASG12D inhibitor with tumor-accumulating pharmacokinetics, drives tumor regression, remodels the immune microenvironment and synergizes with anti–PD-1, and shows promising early clinical responses in lung and pancreatic cancer.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: KRAS G12D is the most prevalent subtype of KRAS mutation across solid tumors, but no drug is available in the clinic. RNK08954 is a potent and selective KRASG12D inhibitor that inhibits proliferation of KRASG12D-mutant cells and demonstrates significant tumor regressions in mouse xenograft models while inhibiting KRAS-mediated signaling. The in vivo effects of RNK08954 are explained by its unique pharmacokinetic (PK) profile and significantly prolonged retention time in tumor tissues. RNK08954 shows synergy with immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). In a phase Ia study, the median follow-up was 4.85 months for 36 evaluable patients. In patients with non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the objective response rate (ORR; unconfirmed) was 58.33%, and in patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the ORR (unconfirmed) was 33.33% in the 1,000- to 1,200-mg cohort. This study supports the clinical potential of RNK08954 in patients with KRASG12D mutation either as a single agent or in combination.

sec.title: Significance:
sec.p: RNK08954 is potentially the first orally bioavailable KRASG12D inhibitor, distinguished by unique PK properties, preclinical efficacy, preliminary clinical activity with encouraging results in patients with NSCLC and PDAC, and synergistic potential with ICB. RNK08954 may address a critical unmet need by targeting the most prevalent KRAS mutation across solid tumors.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The KRAS oncogene, in response to upstream receptor tyrosine kinase activation, is a critical part in the signaling pathways such as MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR and plays a pivotal role in regulating cell proliferation, survival, and differentiation (1, 2). KRAS mutations commonly occur in carcinomas, with activating mutations most commonly occurring as single-nucleotide substitutions in four hotspot codons—12, 13, 61, and 146. Codon 12 is the most frequently mutated of all four hotspot codons, with the G12D mutation generally being the most prevalent, followed by G12V, G12C, and others (3, 4). This mutation disrupts GTPase activity, locking KRAS in a constitutively active GTP-bound state, leading to hyperactivation of downstream oncogenic signaling cascades.

Clinical evidence shows that KRASG12D is most prevalent in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAC), colorectal cancers, and non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC; refs. 5, 6). Oncogenic KRAS signaling has been proved to be more dominant or drive the tumorigenesis in PDAC and lung cancer. In PDAC, KRASG12D mutation is considered one of the earliest events in tumor initiation and promotion (7, 8). Similarly, KRASG12D and KRASG12V are predominant mutations in invasive mucinous lung adenocarcinoma (9, 10). Although colorectal cancer is characterized by extensive heterogeneity with oncogenic alterations in Wnt/APC, BRAF, and PIK3CA, KRAS signaling—as a later genetic event—plays a cooperative role in the process of tumorigenesis (11, 12).

In the past few years, several inhibitors targeting KRASG12C with covalent binding to switch II pocket were approved by the FDA (13) for the treatment of patients with advanced KRASG12C–mutant NSCLC (14–16), thus inspiring parallel strategies for targeting KRASG12D. Currently, emerging approaches targeting KRASG12D include inhibitors (17–21), proteolysis-targeting chimeras (22, 23), and combination therapies targeting downstream effectors or immunotherapy (17, 24–26). These strategies have demonstrated early but modest evidence of activity in the clinical setting. Therefore, targeting KRASG12D continues to present an unmet clinical need (27).

We developed RNK08954, an oral KRASG12D-selective inhibitor. We observed selective binding affinity and KRAS-related signaling (p-ERK1/2) inhibition, which resulted in cell growth inhibition in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, when combined with immunotherapy, RNK08954 induces modulatory effects in the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). Importantly, preliminary evidence of clinical activity of RNK08954 is being demonstrated in the ongoing phase I study (NCT06667544) enrolling patients with KRASG12D mutation. Of interest, all patients enrolled to date with NSCLC have shown evidence of clinical benefit, whereas patients with PDAC showed promising response from a higher dose-level cohort (1,000–1,200 mg).

sec.title: RNK08954 Demonstrates Potent and Selective Inhibition of KRASG12D
sec.p: RNK08954 is a noncovalent inhibitor, targeting KRASG12D. Extensive structure–activity relationship studies facilitated the discovery of RNK08954, which features two potential salt bridge formations between Asp12 (D12) and Glu62 (E62) of KRASG12D and the two basic amino groups of RNK08954, resulting in potent and selective inhibition of KRASG12D (Fig. 1A). Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) was performed to determine the binding affinity of RNK08954 to KRAS protein, and it showed that RNK08954 binds primarily to the inactive KRASG12D (GDP bound) with a dissociation constant (KD) value of 39.5 pmol/L and to the active KRASG12D (GTP bound) form with a KD value of 12.2 nmol/L. The overall binding affinity to KRASG12D protein is higher compared with KRAS wild-type (WT), KRASG12C, and KRASG12V proteins (Fig. 1B).

sec.p: We further performed cellular assays in cell lines with KRASG12D mutation to evaluate the effects of RNK08954 on KRAS signaling and cell viability. Treatment with RNK08954 showed concentration-dependent inhibition of p-ERK1/2 levels in a human pancreatic adenocarcinoma cell line SW1990 as early as 6 hours after treatment, which continued till 72 hours after treatment (Fig. 1C and D). This effect was confirmed by Meso Scale Discovery biomarker assays, which showed significant inhibition of p-ERK1/2, and we found that RNK08954 performed better than MRTX1133 for the value of maximum inhibition and IC50 (Supplementary Fig. S1A). Additionally, RNK08954 demonstrated time- and concentration-dependent inhibition of p-AKT levels (Supplementary Fig. S1B).

Using CellTiter-Glo (CTG) assay, we examined the effect of RNK08954 on cell viability in a panel of cell lines with KRAS mutations that included human cell lines and mouse Ba/F3 cells stably expressing exogenous RAS mutations (Fig. 1E). RNK08954 exhibited potent inhibition, with IC50 values ranging from 2.6 to 49.5 nmol/L in human tumor cells with KRASG12D mutation, and showed selectivity against cells with KRAS WT and other non-G12D KRAS mutations, with the IC50 value of RNK08954 higher than 300 nmol/L. In Ba/F3 cell lines, RNK08954 significantly inhibited cell viability in cells with KRASG12D mutation compared with KRAS WT. From CTG assay, a median IC50 of 10.8 nmol/L was observed with RNK08954 treatment and a median IC50 of 47 nmol/L with MRTX1133. These data indicated that RNK08954 exhibits high activity with markedly higher potency compared with MRTX1133 (Fig. 1E and F). Besides, the treatment of SW1990 cells with RNK08954 induced cell cycle arrest in the G0–G1 phase in a dose-dependent manner and led to cell death (Supplementary Fig. S1C).

sec.title: RNK08954 Preferentially Accumulates in Tumor Tissues
sec.p: Pharmacokinetic (PK) studies in mice were performed to further evaluate the biological effects of RNK08954. Following a single intravenous injection and oral administration of RNK08954 to mice, RNK08954 showed long elimination half-life (T1/2; 7.86 hours) and significantly high volume of distribution (Vss; 36.5 L/kg) at steady state, with oral bioavailability F = 7.56% (Supplementary Table S1).

Additional in vivo studies in GP2d (colon adenocarcinoma) and SW1990 xenograft tumor models in female BALB/c nude mice further supported this observation. As shown in Fig. 2, the ratio of RNK08954 exposure in tumor and plasma (calculated as AUCτ) ranged from 42.5 to 69.7 (Fig. 2A and B), suggesting higher RNK08954 exposure in tumor than that in the plasma. Similarly, in the SW1990 xenograft tumor model, the ratio of RNK08954 exposure in tumor and plasma (calculated as AUCτ) was 22.4 (Fig. 2C and D). Similar to the observation in the GP2d model (Fig. 2A and B), the exposure of RNK08954 in tumor was higher than that in the plasma.

sec.p: High Vss indicates enhanced tissue penetration and tumor exposure more effectively; in line with the rather unique PK profile of RNK08954, significant tumor growth inhibition (TGI) and tumor regression were demonstrated in vivo in the GP2d cell–derived mouse model treated with various dose levels ranging from 10 to 200 mg/kg (orally, twice a day; Fig. 2E). Treatment was tolerated with no significant body weight changes (Fig. 2F).

sec.title: RNK08954 Exhibits Antitumor Activity in KRASG12D-Mutant Cell-Derived Xenograft and Patient-Derived Xenograft Models
sec.p: The antitumor activity of RNK08954 was evaluated in several xenograft mouse models and included A427 (lung adenocarcinoma), SW1990, Panc 04.03 (PDAC), and GP2d, all harboring KRASG12D mutation. RNK08954 was well tolerated in cell-derived xenograft (CDX) models at dosage levels up to 200 mg/kg daily (once daily) in repeat-dose studies for up to 35 days (A427 CDX), with no weight loss, and showed excellent safety profile (Fig. 3A–D; Supplementary Fig. S2A and S2D). RNK08954 significantly inhibited tumor growth in a dose-dependent manner, inducing 70% tumor regression in mice bearing GP2d xenograft administered with 60 mg/kg (once daily) and 100% tumor regression at the 100-mg/kg twice a day dosage in Panc 04.03 xenograft (Fig. 3C and D).

sec.p: The effect of RNK08954 was also studied in pancreatic cancer patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models in female BALB/c nude mice (Fig. 3E–G). RNK08954 was highly effective in inhibiting tumor growth when tested as once daily at a dose of 100 mg/kg (PA1457) or 200 mg/kg (PA1194) or twice a day at a dose of 100 mg/kg (PA1252). Of notion, body weight loss more than 10% was observed in PA1194 and PA1252 mouse models, which might be model specific and because of a low tolerance to higher dose level or dose frequency (Supplementary Fig. S2E and S2F), and mice from PA1457 did not show body weight loss (Supplementary Fig. S2G). The efficacy of RNK08954 was further studied in a human pancreatic cancer (HPAF-II) orthotopic mouse model. Following 28 days of administration, RNK08954 at a dosage of 200 mg/kg once daily led to significant tumor shrinkage compared with the vehicle (Fig. 3H and I). There was no body weight change observed in the study (Supplementary Fig. S2H). Taken together, these results consistently suggest that tumor control and regression are effectively induced by RNK08954 treatment.

sec.title: RNK08954 Inhibits KRAS Signaling and Results in Tumor Regressions In Vivo
sec.p: We then analyzed the PK and pharmacodynamic (PD) profile of RNK08954 using the GP2d xenograft model in BALB/c nude mice. RNK08954 was orally administrated for 5 days at doses of 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg. A dose-dependent increase in plasma and tumor exposure was demonstrated, with a significantly higher differential exposure in the latter (Fig. 4A). The exposure of RNK08954 was approximately 51-fold, 119-fold, and 223-fold higher than that in plasma at 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg, respectively. The elimination of RNK08954 from tumors was relatively slower. The modulation of KRAS downstream signaling included p-ERK and p-S6 levels in tumor tissue after administration (2, 4, 8, and 24 hours). Significant and sustained inhibition of p-ERK was demonstrated at all dose levels. The inhibition of these markers was demonstrated as early as 4 hours and remained through 24 hours after dose (Fig. 4B and C). Similar modulation of p-S6 was also generally seen at the higher dose levels (100 mg/kg; Fig. 4B and D), which may suggest a partial recovery of this pathway at lower dose levels.

sec.p: In the RT-PCR analysis of tumor lysates, a single oral dose of 200 mg/kg RNK08954 resulted in almost 80% inhibition of DUSP6 mRNA expression levels at 24 hours after dosing (Fig. 4E). Consistent with the KRAS signaling inhibition, antitumor activity was also confirmed by daily RNK08954 treatment, which resulted in dose-dependent tumor regression effect in the GP2d CDX model (Supplementary Fig. S3A and S3B). Taken together, these results suggest prolonged exposure in plasma and tumor tissues, with the consequent modulation of KRAS/ERK and KRAS/PI3K signaling pathways and commensurate with TGI.

sec.title: Targeting TIME Enhances Antitumor Activity of RNK08954
sec.p: The effect of RNK08954 on modulation of the TIME was studied in an immunocompetent mouse syngeneic model. RNK08954 administration at a dose of 100 mg/kg exhibited best response in a subcutaneous CT-26–derived mouse syngeneic model (Supplementary Fig. S4A). Immune phenotyping of tumor samples 24 hours after dose using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) demonstrated significant modulation of mouse T cells, B cells, and macrophages (Fig. 5A and B). Further analysis of the T-cell population showed significantly increased CD8+ T-cell population (Fig. 5C and D), as confirmed by flow cytometry analysis with anti-CD3 and anti-CD8 antibodies (Supplementary Fig. S4B, S4C, and S4F). Increased CD8+ T-cell population was also observed in the mouse lung adenocarcinoma cell line syngeneic model (Supplementary Fig. S4D–S4F).

sec.p: The effect of RNK08954 on the TIME was further investigated compared with anti–PD-1 antibody (10 mg/kg) in the same mouse CT-26 syngeneic model. Treatment with RNK08954 as a single agent at a dose of 100 mg/kg significantly inhibited tumor growth compared with either the vehicle group or anti–PD-1 antibody. The combination of RNK08954 and anti–PD-1 antibody further enhanced TGI and tumor regression, with no reduction in body weight (Fig. 5E and F). These effects were further corroborated by the demonstration of modest CD8+ T-cell population expansion with RNK08954 or anti–PD-1 antibody but significant expansion with the combination treatment (Fig. 5G; Supplementary Fig. S5A–S5L). Taken together, these results demonstrate that RNK08954 affects the TIME and leads to the expansion of the CD8+ T population that is required to enhance tumor cell killing. In addition, these results also demonstrate the potential synergistic effects of combining RNK08954 as a KRASG12D inhibitor and a checkpoint inhibitor.

sec.title: RNK08954 Demonstrates Early Evidence of Clinical Activity in Patients
sec.p: Based on the encouraging evidence of in vitro, in vivo, and PK/PD results, a multicenter, open-label, first-in-human phase I clinical study (NCT06667544) was initiated in China, which represents a pivotal step in addressing an unmet clinical need in oncology: targeted therapy for KRASG12D-mutated cancers. The study comprises three parts: phase Ia, a dose-escalation evaluation of safety, tolerability, PK, and preliminary antitumor activity in patients with advanced solid malignancies harboring KRASG12D mutations; phase Ib, a dose-optimization study assessing two dose levels to determine the recommended dose for expansion in phase II; and phase II, an expansion into additional patient populations and cancer subtypes. In phase Ia (Supplementary Table S2), the enrollment of 42 pretreated patients (median prior lines: 2; 17 with PDAC, 14 with NSCLC, four with colorectal cancer, and seven with other KRASG12D-mutant solid tumors) across five flat-dose cohorts (200, 400, 800, 1,000, and 1,200 mg every day) demonstrated the feasibility of this accelerated titration design, reflecting confidence in the drug’s preclinical margin of safety.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: To date (July 21 of 2025), the phase Ia has finished the enrollment of 42 patients, with no dose-limiting toxicities observed in the study up to the final 1,200-mg dose level. All 42 patients (100%) experienced at least one treatment-emergent adverse event (AE; attributable to the study drug (Table 1). The treatment was generally well tolerated with gastrointestinal side effects as the main adverse reactions, and the most common treatment-related AEs were diarrhea (88.1%), vomiting (71.4%), and nausea (66.7%). Most of the reported toxicities were either grade 1 or 2, grade 3, or above, with AEs related to study drug occurring in 10 subjects, with an incidence of 23.8%, including diarrhea in two patients (4.8%), decreased appetite in two patients (4.8%), hypokalemia in two patients (4.8%), and abdominal distension, vomiting, gamma-glutamyl transferase increased, weight decreased, white blood cell count decreased, anemia, asthenia, and pneumonia (one patient, 2.4% for each). Treatment-related AEs resulted in RNK08954 dose modifications: dose interruption in five patients (11.9%), dose reduction five patients (11.9%), and dose permanent discontinuation in one patient (2.1%). Treatment-related AEs that resulted in dose modifications included diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, abdominal pain, pneumonia, increased creatine, hypokalemia, decreased appetite, and asthenia.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: As of the data cutoff on October 20 of 2025, 36 of 42 patients received at least one tumor assessment, and the median time on treatment was 4.85 months for all the patients (range, 1.28–9.23), 5.18 months for NSCLC (range, 2.76–9.23), and 4.86 months for PDAC (1.35–7.85; Fig. 6A). The follow-up duration, progression-free survival, and overall survival will be reported with mature data later. For the two tumor types with the largest number of enrolled subjects, the standout signal emerged in NSCLC. Twelve evaluable patients with NSCLC derived clinical benefit with RNK08954 treatment; of these, seven patients achieved partial response [PR; objective response rate (ORR) of 58.33% and two of seven patients achieved an unconfirmed PR] and five achieved stable disease (SD) according to RECIST 1.1, yielding a disease control rate (DCR) of 100% (Fig. 6B). The preliminary activity observed in NSCLC is notable in a population in which 83% (10 of 12) patients were previously treated with platinum-based chemotherapy and 92% (11 of 12) patients had received immunotherapy. In the PDAC cohort, 13 patients were evaluable with at least one posttreatment tumor assessment, yielding a highly promising interim DCR of 84.62% (two patients with PRs and nine patients with SDs). Notably, both PRs occurred at the 1,200-mg dose cohort, and for the higher dose cohort (1,000–1,200), two patients achieved PR with the ORR of 33.33% (one of two patient achieved an unconfirmed PR) and four achieved SD with DCR of 100%. More importantly, four of six patients from the 1,000- to 1,200-mg cohort are currently in this trial with RNK08954 treatment, which increased the median time on treatment to 6.43 months (range, 4.3–6.87).

sec.title: PK
sec.p: Among 42 patients across tumor types, the steady state was reached by cycle 1 day 8 after multiple-dose administration of RNK08954 once a day. The median tmax,ss was 4, 2, 2, 2, and 2.01 hours from 200 to 1,200 mg, respectively (Supplementary Table S3), indicating rapid absorption of RNK08954. Dose-dependent increases in exposure were observed; the geometric mean Cmax,ss was 27.9, 69.7, 102, 129, and 145 ng/mL from 200 to 1,200 mg respectively, and geometric mean AUCtau,ss was 473, 562, 767, and 990 ng*h/mL for the dose level of 400, 800, 1,000 and 1,200 mg, respectively (Supplementary Table S3; Supplementary Fig. S6). In the range of 400 to 1,200 mg, the exposure to RNK08954 was approximately proportional to the dose increase, and the smaller gain of AUCtau,ss at 1,200 mg suggested a possible plateau and saturation of exposure within clinical dose range. Based on the safety/tolerability, efficacy, and PK data, the doses of 1,000 mg and 1,200 mg administered daily were identified as the recommended dose for the expansion cohort.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The KRASG12D mutation elicits unique structural and signaling properties, drives a highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, and exhibits the most potent oncogenic potential of all KRAS variants (4). However, there are no approved therapies that target KRASG12D, which continues to present a high unmet medical need in several malignancies. KRASG12D has been considered a more challenging target than KRASG12C as it lacks a reactive residue adjacent to the switch II binding pocket (28). Therefore, novel approaches are needed to develop selective inhibitors with drug-like potency and substantial affinity. Significant progress is now being made in the G12D space with the discovery of MRTX1133, which establishes a robust salt bridge between the carboxylic acid side chain of Asp12 and the basic bicyclic amine (29). MRTX1133 is the first noncovalent, potent, and selective KRASG12D inhibitor (1, 20) although recently, Bristol Myers Squibb has announced termination of the development of MRTX1133 because of the high instability of the PK profile. Here, we report that RNK08954 is a highly selective switch II inhibitor against KRASG12D and prefers GDP-bound state, with significant antiproliferative effects on tumor cells and subsequent suppression of downstream ERK1/2 phosphorylation. In addition, RNK08954 has demonstrated favorable PK properties preclinically with oral bioavailability (F: 7.56%), long T1/2 (7.86 hours), and significantly high Vss (36.5 L/kg), which contributed to the excellent antitumor activity in KRASG12D-mutant CDX and PDX models.

There is a high unmet clinical need for patients with PDAC, NSCLC, and other solid tumors with KRASG12D mutation, and the frequency of KRASG12D mutation is 39.5% and 4.9% in PDAC and NSCLC, respectively (5). Recently, Revolution Medicines developed a covalent KRASG12D (on) inhibitor RMC-9805, which forms tri-complex with cyclophilin and KRASG12D. RMC-9805 showed initial antitumor activity in patients with KRASG12D-mutant NSCLC (61% ORR; 89% DCR at high dose level of 1,200 mg; ref. 30) and in PDAC (30% ORR; 80% DCR at 1,200 mg; ref. 31). Additionally, GenFleet Therapeutics reported GFH375, a G12D on/off inhibitor, with antitumor activity in previously treated KRASG12D-mutant NSCLC (57.7% ORR; 88.5% DCR; ref. 32) and in PDAC (42% ORR; 100% DCR with a median follow-up time of 5.65 months; refs. 5, 33). RNK08954 is currently being evaluated in clinical setting with previously treated patients with PDAC, NSCLC, and other solid tumors with KRASG12D mutation. All 12 evaluable patients with KRASG12D-mutant NSCLC derived clinical benefit with RNK08954 treatment; of these, seven patients achieved PR and five achieved SD (58.33% ORR). More importantly, eight patients with NSCLC treated with RNK08954 had detectable KRASG12D at baseline and were evaluable for changes in KRASG12D variant allele frequency (VAF), which showed marked reduction in KRASG12D VAF in ctDNA (Supplementary Fig. S7). For six patients with PDAC with higher dose level (1,000–1,200 mg) of RNK08954, two patients achieved PR with ORR of 33.33% and four achieved SD with DCR of 100%. More importantly, four of six patients with PDAC from the 1,000- to 1,200-mg cohort are currently in this trial with RNK08954 treatment, which increased the median time on treatment to 6.43 months (range, 4.3–6.87) compared with patients from all dose level (4.86 months; range, 1.35–7.85). This encouraging signal suggests potential clinical benefit in PDAC in which historical DCRs rarely exceed 50%. The promising preliminary evidence of clinical activity, particularly in NSCLC and PDAC, and the favorable tolerability provide a strong rational for further testing. Currently, phase Ib dose optimization in cohort A (PDAC), cohort B (NSCLC), and other solid tumors (cohort 3) is recruiting with RNK08954 at 1,000- to 1,200-mg dose level; RNK08954 will be further studied in phase Ib and phase II.

The study demonstrated that the synergistic effect in combination with anti–PD-1 antibody increases the CD8+ T-cell infiltration in the TIME, and this suggested that KRASG12D inhibition would facilitate the activity of anti–PD-1. Several recent studies suggest that KRASG12D is a major culprit in promoting an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Indeed, the inhibition of KRASG12D stimulates specific, potent, and durable tumor regressions in the KPC pancreatic cancer model (25). A recent study revealed that KRASG12D inhibition with the inhibitor MRTX1133 increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration and reprogramed cancer-associated fibroblasts. In other studies, KRASG12D mutation was found to correlate with low tumor mutation burden and immune suppression (low CD8+PD-1+ T cells and low PD-L1 expression on tumor and immune cells) in NSCLC (34). Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been reported to have suboptimal efficacy in patients with NSCLC with KRASG12D (35). Immune-deserted and immune-exhausted tumors with low T-cell infiltration may require prolonged drug exposure for immune modulation. The selective inhibition of KRASG12D and the observed high Vss of RNK08954, leading to potentially prolonged drug exposure, thus provide a plausible rationale for this combination strategy in patients with PD-1 expression, particularly in PDAC and NSCLC.

In conclusion, RNK08954 is a selective noncovalent KRASG12D inhibitor that demonstrated high efficacy in KRASG12D-mutant cancers in vitro and in vivo. RNK08954 is demonstrating evidence of clinical activity in the ongoing phase I study and warrants additional testing in specific tumor indications, either as a single agent or in combination. If successful, RNK08954 will add to the growing list of drugs targeting KRAS mutations and could potentially present a new paradigm change.

The cell lines were incubated in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2 at 37°C. sec.title: Cell Proliferation Inhibition Assay (CTG 2.0 Assay, Promega, G9243)
sec.p: In the cell growth inhibition experiments, each tested compound was serially diluted in threefold, 10 doses. The diluted compounds were transferred into a 384-well cell plate and cells were seeded. Some wells were kept empty for no cell control (containing only medium) and also served as a control for the CTG signal. After the addition of the cells, the plate was agitated on a plate shaker at 600 rpm for 1 to 2 minutes and then incubated for 24 hours or 72 hours at 37°C in an incubator with 5% CO2 before adding CTG reagent. After the CTG 2.0 Assay reagent was added equally to the culture medium in each well, the plates were shaken at room temperature for 10 minutes. The luminescence was read on the Ensight Tecan Infinite M Plex microplate reader (RRID: SCR_026522) and the IC50 was calculated by fitting the curve using XLfit (v5. 3. 1. 3) using the formula % inhibition = 100% − 100% × (signal sample − signal LC/signal HC-signal LC).

sec.title: SPR
sec.p: The target proteins (WT KRAS-GDP, KRAS G12D-GCP/GDP, KRAS G12C-GDP, and KRAS G12V-GDP) were first diluted with buffer (10 mmol/L HEPES, 150 mmol/L NaCl, 0.05% Tween 20, 5 mmol/L MgCl2, 0.5 mmol/L Tris (2-carboxy-ethyl)-phosphin-HCl, and 1 μmol/L GDP/GCP) at 25°C to 10 μg/mL and coupled onto the surface of the CAP chip. The compounds to be tested were then gradient diluted and titrated through the chip surface in the ascending order of concentration. The samples were subjected to Biacore 8K+ (GE Healthcare Bio-Sciences AB). Finally, the association and dissociation curve of the compound against the target was obtained. The affinity and kinetic constants can be determined accordingly.

sec.title: Western Blot Assay
sec.p: Cells were collected and lysed with RIPA lysis buffer (Boston BioProducts, BP-115D) containing the protease/phosphatase inhibitor (cOmplete ULTRA Tablets, Roche Applied Science, 05892791001; phosphatase inhibitor cocktail, Roche Applied Science, 04906837001), and the samples were further subjected to bicinchoninic acid quantification. The samples were heated with 5X SDS loading buffer before running electrophoresis (gel, Invitrogen, WXP42026BOX). The membranes were incubated with the indicated primary antibody and secondary antibody after protein transfer (NC membrane, Millipore, HATF00010) and blocking with LICOR buffer (LICORbio, 927-50000) for 1 hour. The membranes were exposed using Odyssey CLx (LICORbio, RRID: SCR_014579).

sec.title: PDX
sec.p: Female BALB/c nude mice (RRID: IMSR_RJ: BALB-C-NUDE) aged 6 to 8 weeks were inoculated subcutaneously in the right front flank with PA1252/PA1457/PA1194 human pancreatic cancer PDX model tumor fragments (approximately 2–3 mm in diameter). A total of 12 animals were randomly assigned to three groups after inoculation, with four mice/group, and the mean tumor volumes of each group were ∼313 (PA1252), 291 (PA457), and 206 (PA1194) mm3. Mice were treated with vehicle (10% SBE-β-CD in 10 mmol/L citrate buffer, pH 5) or RNK08954 at a dose of 100 or 200 mg/kg (every day or twice a day). The mice were administered via oral gavage (every day) twice daily for 23 consecutive days (PA1252/PA1457) or 25 consecutive days (PA1194). Tumor volumes and body weights were measured two times per week. Tumor volume was measured by caliper measurements along two orthogonal axes and calculated with a formula of V (mm3) = (length × width2)/2. The tumor volume ratio (T/C) and TGI compared with the vehicle-treated control group were calculated and statistically analyzed.

The protocol and any amendment(s) or procedures involving the care and use of animals in this study were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Crown Bioscience prior to execution. During the study, the care and use of animals were conducted in accordance with the regulations of the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care (AAALAC).

sec.title: CDX
sec.p: BALB/c nude mice (SW1990/GP2d) or NOD/SCID mice (RRID: IMSR_JAX:005557; A427/Panc04.03/HPAF-II-luc) aged 6 to 8 weeks were obtained from GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. Mice were reared in groups with free access to food and water under a 12:12 light–dark cycle at 23°C ± 3°C. The mice were subcutaneously injected with cells to establish the xenograft model in mice. When the tumor volume reached 100 to 200 mm3, the mice were randomly divided into four groups (n = 4–8). The compounds were administered orally every day or twice a day for 3 to 4 weeks, and in selected cohorts exhibiting strong antitumor responses, treatment and tumor monitoring were extended beyond 28 days to assess the potential for further tumor regression and durability of response, in compliance with institutional animal care guidelines. The body weight and tumor volume were measured every 2 to 3 days. Tumor volume was measured by caliper measurements along two orthogonal axes and calculated with a formula of V (mm3) = (length × width2)/2. The images from HPAF-II-luc xenograft mice were obtained by IVIS Lumina series III (RRID: SCR_025239).

sec.title: Syngeneic Mouse Model
sec.p: BALB/c mice (RRID: MGI:2161072) aged 6 to 8 weeks were obtained from SPF Biotechnology Ltd. The mice were subcutaneously injected with cells to establish the xenograft model in mice. When the tumor volume reached 100 to 200 mm3, the mice were randomly divided into four groups (n = 4). Compounds were orally administrated every day for 3 weeks, and the body weight and tumor volume were measured every 2 to 3 days. Tumor volume was measured by caliper measurements along two orthogonal axes and calculated with a formula of V (mm3) = (length × width2)/2.

Animal experiments were conducted by Pharmaron Beijing Co., Ltd., under their IACUC approval (ON-CELL-XEN-06012022). All the procedures in this study related to animal handling, care, and the treatment were performed according to guidelines approved by the IACUC of Pharmaron following the guidance of the AAALAC. sec.title: PK Profile
sec.p: CD1/male mice (RRID: IMSR_CRL:022; Beijing Vital River Experimental Animal Technology Co., Ltd) received the intravenous and oral doses of RNK08954. RNK08954 was administered intravenously at a dose of 5 mg/kg or orally at a dose of 60 mg/kg (three mice per group). RNK08954 was formulated in 10% (w/v) sulfobutyl ether-β-cyclodextrin sodium (10% SBECD). Blood samples from animals in the intravenous groups were collected at 0.0833, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours after dose and in the oral groups at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours after dose. The plasma concentrations of RNK08954 were determined by a qualified LC/MS-MS method with the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) of 1 ng/mL for RNK08954. Within 30 minutes of collection, all samples were centrifuged at 4,000 g for 5 minutes at 4°C to obtain plasma. The resultant plasma samples were stored in polypropylene tubes, quickly frozen in ice box, and stored in a freezer set to maintain −75°C ± 15°C or colder until SCIEX API 4000 LC/MS-MS System (RRID: SCR_026454) analysis. Phoenix WinNonlin version 8.3 (Phoenix 64, Build 8.3.4.295) was used for calculating the descriptive statistics and the PK parameters, as well as the figures and tables. Individual RNK08954 plasma concentrations were used to calculate the PK parameters by noncompartmental analysis (NCA, WinNonlin, RRID: SCR_024504), and mean PK parameters were calculated from individual animals.

sec.title: Tissue Distribution of RNK08954 in Tumor-Bearing Mice
sec.p: Female BALB/c nude mice were inoculated subcutaneously in the right hind flank with SW1990 tumor cells plus Matrigel (1:1)/100 μL resuspended in serum-free DMEM culture medium. Mice were treated with RNK08954 at a dose of 100 mg/kg. The mice were administered orally once daily for 14 consecutive days, respectively. Blood and tumor samples were collected at 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours after the last dose with three mice per time point.

Female BALB/c nude mice were inoculated subcutaneously in the right hind flank with GP2d tumor cells plus Matrigel (1:1)/100 μL resuspended in serum-free DMEM culture medium and randomly assigned to three groups. Mice were treated with RNK08954 at doses of 20, 60, or 200 mg/kg, respectively. The mice were administered via oral administration once daily for 14 consecutive days. Blood and tumor samples were collected at 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours after the last dose with three mice per time point.

The plasma and tumor concentrations of RNK08954 were determined by a qualified LC/MS-MS method with the LLOQ of 1 ng/mL for RNK08954. PK parameters were calculated by using NCA with WinNonlin (8.0.0.3176) to assess the characteristics of RNK08954 in female BALB/c nude mice.

sec.title: PK and PD Assays
sec.p: A total of 180 female BALB/c nude mice were inoculated subcutaneously in the right hind flank with 1 × 107 GP2d tumor cells plus Matrigel (1:1)/100 μL resuspended in culture medium. On the 10th and 17th day after inoculation, a total of 72 female BALB/c nude mice bearing GP2d tumors were selected and randomly assigned to seven groups, with vehicle group (six mice/group), treatment group (12 mice/group), and the mean tumor volumes of each group being ∼281 and ∼411 mm3, respectively. Mice were treated with vehicle (10% SBECD in pure water) or RNK08954 at doses of 10, 30, or 100 mg/kg per dose. The mice were administered via oral gavage once daily for five consecutive days or a single dose, respectively. Tumor volume and body weight were measured once daily. The relationship between changes in mouse body weight and tumor volume and time of administration were recorded. The T/C, TGI, and tumor regression rate compared with the vehicle-treated control group were calculated and statistically analyzed. Plasma and tumors were harvested at 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours after the last dose and at 2 and 24 hours only for the vehicle group. Each tumor was cut into three to four pieces. Twenty-five percent of each tumor was analyzed by Western blotting with p-ERK and p-S6 antibodies, 25% for the expression of DUSP6 by qPCR, and 25% for RNK08954 exposure (PK). Plasma was also analyzed for PK.

sec.title: RT-PCR of DUSP6
sec.p: RNA was extracted according to instructions of the MagMAX mirVana Total RNA Isolation Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A27828). Reverse transcription reaction was carried out using the QuantiTect Reverse Transcription Kit (Qiagen, 205314) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The cDNA product was used for qPCR analysis using TaqMan FAST Gene Expression Master Mix (Invitrogen, 4444557). TaqMan primer probes specific to DUSP6 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Hs00737962_m1) were used, and β-actin was used as an internal control gene (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Hs01060665_g1) and assayed on a Life Technologies QuantStudio 5 Real-Time PCR System (RRID: SCR_020240). Data were analyzed using the 2−ΔΔCt method with actin and are presented as relative expression compared with vehicle. Means ± SEM are shown.

sec.title: Tumor Tissue Digestion and scRNA-seq
sec.p: Samples were from CT-26 (RRID: CVCL_7254) syngeneic mouse model efficacy with RNK08954. The digestive solution for tumor tissues was prepared by mixing 1 mg/mL collagenase type II (Gibco, 17101-015) with 0.1 mg/mL DNase I (Merck, 10104159001) and then dissolved in RPMI-1640 medium. Digestion was carried out at 37°C for 1 hour on a shaker. At the end of digestion, the solution was filtered through 70-μm filters and centrifuged at 1,500 rpm for 5 minutes. Precipitated cells were lysed with 1 mL of red blood cell lysate for 3 minutes at room temperature and centrifuged at 1,500 rpm for 5 minutes. The supernatant was discarded, washed with 1 mL of PBS, and centrifuged at 1,500 rpm for 5 minutes. Tumor tissue cells isolated from the vehicle and RNK8954-treated groups were mixed three times each, and CD45+ sorting of tumor tissue cells was performed using a Beckman Coulter CytoFLEX S V4-B2-Y4-R3 Flow Cytometer (RRID: SCR_027083), and the sorted lymphocytes were subjected to scRNA-seq analysis. A total of 8,783 cells were obtained from the vehicle group, which were filtered to obtain 7,943 high-quality cells. A total of 7,604 cells were obtained from the RNK08954 treatment group, which were filtered to obtain 6,938 high-quality cells. The single-cell suspension obtained previously was then loaded onto the 10x Genomics Chromium X Single Cell Analyzer (RRID: SCR_024537) to capture single cells based on the manufacturer’s instructions of the 10x Genomics Chromium Single-Cell 3′ kit (V3). A standard protocol was followed in amplifying cDNA and constructing the library. The library was sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 Sequencing System (paired-end multiplexing run, 150 bp) by LC-Bio Technology Co., Ltd. at a depth of at least 20,000 reads per cell. Detailed information on RNK08954 synthesis and methods related to supplementary figures is provided in Supplementary Materials and Methods S1.

sec.title: Clinical Trial
sec.p: The RNK08954 clinical trial (NCT06667544) is currently being conducted in accordance with established ethical guidelines (Declaration of Helsinki) and per local institutional review board guidelines. Each patient included in the clinical trial provided written informed consent form prior to their participation in the study. RNK08954 was administered once daily in 21-day cycles until evidence of objective disease progression or withdrawal due intolerable toxicity or withdrawal from study.

sec.p: Dose escalation/deescalation is guided by the U-BOIN design. The first dose group (200 mg) starts with one subject using accelerated titration. Subsequent dose groups enroll at least three subjects each. After all subjects in a dose group complete the evaluable DLT observation period (3 weeks), the dose for the next group is determined based on the dose-escalation/deescalation rules described in the dose-escalation principles. Depending on the toxicity profile of RNK08954, the total number of phase Ia subjects enrolled at a given dose may vary, but no more than 12 subjects will be enrolled at any dose. Approximately 42 subjects are expected to participate in the phase Ia trial.
